newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Soldiers to keep peace at HK-Japan soccer match.
newsitem.headline: Soldiers to keep peace at HK-Japan soccer match.

text.p: Hong Kong authorities, fearing anti-Japanese sentiment could whip soccer fans into a frenzy, will deploy British soldiers to keep the peace at a match later this month between Japanese and Hong Kong teams, organisers said on Friday.
The precautions were intended to head off any outbreak of violence linked to the wave of protests over a group of East China Sea islands held by Japan but also claimed by China.
"Definitely they (British army soldiers) will be helping us man the stadium," said spokeswoman Julia Lau of Wembley International (Hong Kong), which manages Hong Kong Stadium.
"The number (of soldiers) depends on the situation, the number of Japanese fans, Hong Kong spectators," Lau said.
The soldiers would trade fatigues for steward uniforms as part of a security team that could reach 300. The usual non-military security force numbers 150.
Hong Kong police also would boost their presence from a usual 30 or so to 175, Lau said.
"The first five rows of seats will not be sold, to increase the distance between the spectators and the pitch," she said.

Metal fences will skirt the pitch to protect players, and Japanese fans will be seated in a sectioned-off area of the stands, protected by extra security guards. Organisers were also considering separate entrances.
The match -- between Japan's Grampas 8 and Hong Kong's South China side -- was also postponed from October 20 to October 22, but Lau could not give the reason for the switch.
Anti-Japanese sentiment has flared in Chinese communities in Hong Kong, China, Taiwan and Macau since a Japanese rightist group built a lighthouse on the rocky islets in July.
Tokyo's claim to what it calls the Senkakus dates from 1895. China and political rival Taiwan also have claimed the islands, calling them the Diaoyus.

Anger hit a new high last week when a Hong Kong activist drowned after jumping off a ship to protest Japan's sovereignty claim over the islands. Tens of thousands of people turned out to mourn him in Hong Kong last Sunday.
Daily ritual protests continued on Friday when a small group of activists gathered outside a downtown Japanese department store and shouted for a boycott of Japanese goods.
